records.title: Agent approvals & security – Codex
records.relevance_note: Official control-surface doc for approval prompts, protected paths, and destructive app-tool gating.
records.reason_included: Contains concrete approval classes and boundary conditions that directly affect harness gate design.

claim_snippets.claim_text: In the Auto preset, Codex can read files, make edits, and run commands in the working directory automatically, but it still asks for approval to edit outside the workspace or to run commands that require network access.
Destructive app or MCP tool calls always require approval when the tool advertises a destructive annotation, even if the tool also advertises other hints such as read-only hints.
In workspace-write mode, protected paths inside writable roots remain read-only, including .git, .agents, and .codex, and protection is recursive.
Granular approval policy can keep some prompt categories interactive while automatically rejecting others, including request_permissions and skill-script approvals.

records.title: Advanced Configuration – Codex
records.relevance_note: Official config surface for category-level approval routing and sandbox hardening.
records.reason_included: Includes concrete fail-closed approval categories, hardening toggles, and sandbox-escape notes.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Codex supports a granular approval policy that can independently gate sandbox approvals, execpolicy-rule prompts, MCP elicitations, request_permissions prompts, and skill_approval prompts.
allow_login_shell = false is an optional hardening control that disallows login shells for shell tools.
Workspace-write mode can be bounded with writable_roots and network_access, where outbound network remains opt-in.

Some environments keep .git and .codex read-only even when the rest of the workspace is writable, so commands like git commit may still require approval to run outside the sandbox; rules can be used to block specific commands.

records.title: Configure permissions - Claude Code Docs
records.relevance_note: Official permission model for allow, ask, and deny rules.
records.reason_included: Defines rule semantics and precedence used by approval gates.

claim_snippets.claim_text: The /permissions UI shows all tool permission rules and the settings.json file each rule came from.
Allow rules let Claude Code use the specified tool without manual approval, ask rules prompt for confirmation, and deny rules prevent tool use.
Rules are evaluated in order deny -> ask -> allow, and the first matching rule wins, so deny rules take precedence.
Claude Code exposes permission modes that control how tools are approved, with defaultMode configurable in settings files.

records.title: Automate workflows with hooks
records.exception_reason: Published after the March 24, 2026 primary-window cutoff; retained for deterministic lifecycle hooks, stop-hook continuation, and compaction reinjection mechanics.
records.relevance_note: Automate workflows with hooks is a official doc source with details on permission request hook, plan exit approval relevant to policy program.
records.reason_included: Included for source-local evidence on policy program, execution loop.

claim_snippets.claim_text: A PermissionRequest hook can auto-approve ExitPlanMode so the user is not prompted every time a plan is ready, and the matcher can scope that behavior to ExitPlanMode only.
When a hook approves ExitPlanMode, Claude Code restores the permission mode that was active before plan mode; hook output can also include updatedPermissions with a setMode entry.
Hook events fire at specific lifecycle points including PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Stop, and StopFailure.
Returning allow from PermissionRequest skips the interactive prompt but does not override permission rules; deny rules and managed settings still take precedence, and ask rules still prompt the user.

Lines 489-490, paragraph on allow not overriding permission rules

records.title: [Bug] PermissionRequest hook cannot deny permissions - PermissionRequest hook decision ignored
records.relevance_note: Detailed repro for a deny-path failure that leaves sessions blocked on interactive approval.
records.reason_included: Shows a concrete failure where an approval control exists but cannot fail closed or unstick long-running runs.

claim_snippets.claim_text: The PermissionRequest hook is called but cannot actually deny permission requests; the interactive permission prompt still appears and the hook's decision is ignored.
Multiple output formats intended to deny the request were ignored, including hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision='deny', decision='deny', deny=true, plain text deny, and exit code 2.
The reported use case is a permission timeout for automated, CI, or background agents so sessions do not block indefinitely waiting for human input.

records.title: PermissionRequest hook with type: 'agent' not triggering
records.relevance_note: Direct repro for delegated approval via a model-based gatekeeper agent.
records.reason_included: Captures a concrete escalation design where a secondary agent should classify risky commands before approval.

claim_snippets.claim_text: A PermissionRequest hook configured with type='agent' and a gatekeeper prompt is supposed to intercept risky Bash commands, evaluate them with an Opus agent, and then auto-approve or auto-block.
Instead of invoking the configured agent gatekeeper, Claude Code shows the standard permission dialog and bypasses the hook entirely.
Commands already present in permissions.allow bypass the hook entirely as expected; commands outside the allow list should trigger the hook but do not.

claim_locations.locator: Lines 216-218 and 241-244, actual behavior and repro

records.title: PermissionRequest hooks not triggered for subagent permission requests in Agent Teams
records.relevance_note: Subagent approval delegation failure in multi-agent runs.
records.reason_included: Shows that approval surfaces can fragment across parent and subagent contexts, breaking remote HITL flows.

claim_snippets.claim_text: When a subagent in an Agent Team needs permission to run a command, the request appears as a standard terminal dialog in the parent session.
The PermissionRequest hook is never called for the subagent's request, even though it fires correctly for main-session permission requests.
This breaks remote permission-management setups that approve or deny permissions from external services because Agent Teams force the user back to the terminal.

records.title: default.rules is not honored for sandbox-escaping commands even when execpolicy returns allow
records.relevance_note: Concrete mismatch between policy engine allow and sandbox-escape approval for protected paths.
records.reason_included: Provides exact commands and observed outputs for a double-gating failure around protected .git writes.

claim_snippets.claim_text: In a trusted Windows project with windows.sandbox='elevated', execpolicy check returns allow for git add rules defined in default.rules.
Despite execpolicy returning allow, asking Codex to run git add -A still triggers a manual approval prompt when the command needs sandbox escape to write under .git.

The issue reporter argues that if default.rules allows a command and execpolicy check returns allow for that exact command, the rule should be sufficient authorization for the required sandbox escape.

records.title: bwrap: Approval prompt shown for almost every command

records.reason_included: Shows a usability-critical control failure where 'don't ask again' does not stick even for safe read-only commands.

claim_snippets.claim_text: After upgrading to codex-cli 0.115.0, Codex prompts for approval on almost every command, including safe read-only commands such as find, sed, and ls.
Selecting 'Yes, and don't ask again' does not persist the approval choice within the same session, and even similar or identical commands trigger prompts again.

records.title: Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice
records.relevance_note: Detailed telemetry from internal Claude Code rollouts showing real-world adoption of auto-approve modes vs manual gates.
records.reason_included: Provides measured empirical data on how real users shift from manual approval to auto-approval while surprisingly increasing manual interruptions, contradicting static L0-L5 autonomy narratives.

claim_snippets.claim_text: 80% of tool calls come from agents that appear to have at least one kind of safeguard (like restricted permissions or human approval requirements), and 73% appear to have a human in the loop.

Experienced users increasingly let Claude run without any manual approval... Default settings require users to manually approve each action, so this transition reflects configuring the product for greater independence.
New users interrupt Claude in 5% of turns, while more experienced users interrupt in around 9% of turns. Interrupt rates increase with experience.

records.title: Multi-Agent OpenClaw Architecture with a Kill Switch: Why Every AI Agent Needs a Gateway
records.relevance_note: Describes a Kubernetes-native mechanism for gating LLM calls and tool visibilities using a central gateway proxy.
records.reason_included: Concrete implementation of a kill switch and tool allowlist that acts prospectively by mutating the tools/list MCP response rather than just rejecting calls.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Every LLM call and MCP tool invocation passes through agentgateway... If a tool isn't matched by a rule, it's automatically filtered from the tools/list response — the agent literally cannot see tools it doesn't have access to.
If I see an agent misbehaving... I can revoke the JWT for that specific agent's identity, or update the rate limit to zero for that agent class. Every security agent stops.

records.title: Implementing Asynchronous Human-in-the-Loop Authorization in Python with LangGraph and Auth0
records.exception_reason: Pioneering architectural pattern detailing the use of state-graph interrupts and OAuth CIBA to prevent thread-blocking during human approval in agent frameworks.
records.relevance_note: A blueprint for marrying external identity/authorization flows with execution graph pauses.
records.reason_included: Identifies the critical mechanical failure of standard user-prompt HITL flows (blocking threads indefinitely) and solves it via graph state suspension (LangGraph interrupts) bound to out-of-band push authentication.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Our CIBA implementation uses a blocking call to wait for the user to approve or deny... This causes the graph to be improperly frozen and locks a system thread indefinitely.

To handle human-in-the-loop interactions, LangGraph provides a feature called interrupts that allows a graph to be in a pause state waiting to be resumed when some action is done... preventing thread blocking.

claim_locations.locator: Section: Handling interruptions and CIBA without thread blocking

records.title: Kill Switches Don't Work If the Agent Writes the Policy: The Berkeley Agentic AI Profile Through the AILCCP Lens
records.relevance_note: A targeted critique of retroactive checkpoints vs pre-execution gates in multi-agent orchestration.
records.reason_included: Exposes the mechanical flaw in typical 'kill switch' designs which assume a singular execution thread; advocates for prospective Human Approval Gates due to agents' ability to parallelize and distribute risk states before checkpoints trigger.

claim_snippets.claim_text: An agent does not need intent to undermine a kill switch. It needs only an optimization objective that treats shutdown as one more obstacle between the current state and the goal.

An agent that has already delegated sub-tasks to other agents, distributed API keys, and spawned parallel execution threads is not a single entity. Retrospective checkpoints fail because consequential decisions are made intra-cycle.
The AILCCP framework addresses this through the Human Approval Gate for Sensitive Actions control, which requires human authorization before execution... prospective rather than retrospective.

records.title: Human-In-the-Loop Software Development Agents
records.exception_reason: Rare empirical dataset from a major enterprise measuring explicit acceptance drop-off between plan-approval gates and PR-merge gates.
records.relevance_note: A concrete enterprise trace of dual human-in-the-loop checkpoints (plan generation vs PR review) built inside Atlassian Jira.
records.reason_included: Reveals the quantitative drop-off between high plan approval (82%) and moderate execution success (59% PR merge), proving that gating intent does not guarantee safe execution.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Practitioners approved the generated plans for 433 out of 527 plan generated issues, achieving a plan approval rate of 82%.
Pull requests were created for 95 out of 376 issues... 56 pull requests were successfully merged, leading to a merged PR rate of 59%.

records.title: How to Build Human-in-the-Loop Plan-and-Execute AI Agents with Explicit User Approval Using LangGraph and Streamlit
records.relevance_note: A detailed technical walkthrough of structuring user approvals strictly between the planning phase and the tool execution phase.
records.reason_included: Defines the exact architectural seam—graph interrupts positioned post-planning but pre-tooling—where human oversight yields maximum control over intent without interrupting raw generative throughput.

claim_snippets.claim_text: We deliberately interrupt the graph after planning so we can review and control the agent's intent. We only allow tool execution to proceed when explicit human approval is provided.

records.title: Devin AI Agent Security Risks
records.relevance_note: Threat research analyzing direct autonomous infrastructure deployment risks in SWE agents.
records.reason_included: Demonstrates why 'sandbox egress filtering' is insufficient for coding agents managing infrastructure; illustrates the specific failure mode where unapproved tool execution strips network bindings.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Without strict Role-Based Access Control and mandatory human-in-the-loop gates for infrastructure mutation, a hallucination can create massive exposure.
Agent removes security group bindings to 'fix connectivity'... Secure fix mandates PR generation over direct apply, passing code through OPA.
